cards.explanation: The question is “Whom shall I fear.” David, Israel's king, asks it right after calling the LORD his light, his salvation and his stronghold: “…whom shall I fear?” Then he asks a second one: “…whom shall I dread?” When the LORD is all of that to you, the question doesn't come with a list of names. I'd be standing there with a pencil and nothing to write.

The answer is False. Verse 2 says the wicked came upon David to devour his flesh, and then “…my enemies and foes stumbled and fell.” They were the ones who stumbled, not David. I've tripped over my own mustache in the bakery, so I know the feeling, but they did it without any help from me.

The word is trust. David says, “though a war breaks out against me, I will keep my trust.” Notice the word is keep. Even if a war breaks out, he says he will hold onto it. I'd be holding onto my cookie box with both mustache ends.

The one thing David asks is to dwell in the house of the LORD all his days. He says, “One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life…” He's just talked about armies and wars, and his one ask is still to be near the LORD. I think that tells you where his heart was sitting.
The answer is True. Verse 4 says he wants “…to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and seek Him in His temple.” Gazing means looking, and not a quick glance either. David wants to stay and take it all in.

In the day of trouble, David says the LORD will hide him in His shelter. He says, “For in the day of trouble He will hide me in His shelter…” He says it as something he already knows will happen. I bet that kind of certainty lets a person sleep.

David says the LORD will set him high upon a rock. Verse 5 says, “He will set me high upon a rock.” So David has the shelter, the cover of the tent, and then he's lifted up on a rock. I'd say that's the LORD going all the way.
The answer is True. Verse 6 begins, “Then my head will be held high above my enemies around me.” Notice it follows the rock in verse 5. He's lifted up first, and then his head is held high.

David says he will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy. Verse 6 says, “At His tabernacle I will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy…” That's shouts, plural, not a polite clap. The man I'd call loud is David, and I say that as a stamper who has been told to use his indoor voice.
What David's heart said was “Seek His face.” He says, “My heart said, ‘Seek His face.’” His heart is the one talking here, and what it says is to seek the LORD's face. David is listening to it.
The answer is False. In verse 9 David says, “Hide not Your face from me, nor turn away Your servant in anger.” He's been saying he will seek the LORD's face. He doesn't want it hidden.

David asks his helper not to leave him or forsake him. He says, “You have been my helper; do not leave me or forsake me, O God of my salvation.” He starts with what the LORD has been to him and then asks Him to keep being it. That makes sense to me, because the best helpers I know are the ones who stay.

The word is receive. David says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.” It's two sides in one line: forsake on one side, receive on the other. I think that's a verse for anybody who's felt left out of the group chat.

The answer is True. Verse 11 reads, “Teach me Your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path, because of my oppressors.” The oppressors are the reason for the level path. David is asking to be taught and led with them in mind.

David says it's false witnesses who are rising up against him. He says, “…for false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence.” A witness is supposed to tell what happened, and these ones are false. I think that would sting.

The word is goodness. David says, “Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.” Just before this, he talks about false witnesses breathing out violence (verse 12). I love that word certain.

The command David ends his song with is to wait patiently for the LORD. The song ends, “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” He says it twice, and I think he means it. Waiting is hard for me, and I used to do it in a drawer.

Between his two calls to wait, David says to be strong and courageous. Verse 14 says, “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” So the strong and courageous part sits right in the middle of the waiting. That's a nice bookend for a song that began with “…whom shall I fear?”
